description_full: Fastenal Company, together with its subsidiaries, engages in the wholesale distribution of industrial and construction supplies in the United States, Canada, Mexico, and internationally. It offers fasteners, and related industrial and construction supplies under the Fastenal name. The company's fastener products include threaded fasteners, bolts, nuts, screws, studs, and related washers that are used in manufactured products and construction projects, as well as in the maintenance and repair of machines. It offers miscellaneous supplies and hardware, including pins, machinery keys, concrete anchors, metal framing systems, wire ropes, strut products, rivets, and related accessories. The company serves the manufacturing market comprising original equipment manufacturers; maintenance, repair, and operations customers; non-residential construction market; farmers, truckers, railroads, mining companies, schools, and retail trades; and oil exploration, production, and refinement companies, as well as federal, state, and local governmental entities. Fastenal Company was founded in 1967 and is headquartered in Winona, Minnesota.

financial_summary: Fastenal Company is a large-cap industrials business with a $61.3B market cap on $8.2B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +6% over the past three years and +8% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size.
Returns on capital run at 33% against a 9% cost of capital — a 24-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat, with gross margins sitting at 49%.

The business throws off $1.1B in free cash flow — roughly 13 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.03× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year.

Shareholder yield is only 1.6%, a thin return of capital, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 1.8× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

Cyclicality and capital intensity — order books turn on a dime, and the heavy fixed cost base that creates the moat also magnifies the downturn.
Supply chain reshoring costs and labour shortages — onshoring mandates raise capex requirements while a shrinking skilled-labour pool inflates operating costs.
Tariff and trade-policy exposure — industrial exporters sit squarely in the crosshairs of protectionist policy, and retaliatory tariffs can close markets without warning.

sect: Its 20% operating margin runs 11pp above the Industrials median (9%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 1.81x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
It accounts for 0.2% of sector revenue and 0.4% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-4.1% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.01 across 550 companies in the universe; the top four hold 9% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 30% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the top of its 52-week range, 5% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 25% and a beta of 0.83, it moves roughly with the market.
Liquidity is deep, with about $333.0M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 28% in the 2020 crash, 28% in the 2022 bear market and 52% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $23.42 (margin of safety -128%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models corroborate one another (dispersion 5%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $12.14 to $46.26 (P10-P90).
On multiples it looks expensive against Industrials peers: P/E 43.4 vs 23.1, EV/EBITDA 30.1 vs 13.3 and P/FCF 58.3 vs 22.4 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 94% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 1.7% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 2.7% (vs the 8% bar).
The 13 covering analysts target $50.76 on average, 5% below the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 33% clears the cost of capital of 8.7% by 24pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have been steady (CV 0.14).
It runs a 49% gross margin and converts 13% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: a Piotroski score of 7/9 and cash conversion of 1.03x.
ROE of 32% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.3x equity multiplier).
It spends 0.1% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $151.8M (0% of market cap).
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 37.6, in the safe zone).
Working capital ties up about 171 days of sales, a drag on cash generation.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 5.5% over 3 years, 7.7% over 5 years and 7.8% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating.
At current returns, reinvesting 24% of profits supports about 7.8% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 2.4% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.4x, 3.0% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 20, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
Analysts expect 10.9% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.1%), and institutions hold 89%.
Insiders have only sold over the past year (8 sales, net $5.0M sold).
Shareholder yield is a modest 1.6% (1.9% in dividends).
It has paid a dividend for 34 consecutive years, raising it 4.6% a year over the last five.
people: With about 21,749 employees, each generates about $377K of revenue, in line with the Industrials median, and revenue has grown 9.5% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $48K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $2.4M (6x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores poorly (9/10, lower is better).
